paras: The reported lynching of Frank Lane was the reported seizure and killing by a mob of a man accused of stabbing two card players at Mountainburg, Arkansas, on the night of August 24, 1882. A wire dispatch from Alma said only that Lane was in a mob's hands and believed already lynched, and no report found confirms his fate. The dispatch nonetheless circulated nationally, and some roundups reported the lynching as fact.

According to the dispatch, Tom Simcoe, David Pope and Frank Lane quarreled over a game of cards at Mountainburg. The Harrison Times, an Arkansas weekly, placed the fight at Porters Station on the 'Frisco road near Mountainburg, called it a "general free fight" and blamed "Cards and whisky."

Lane was said to have drawn a knife, cut Pope in the abdomen, "disemboweling him," and then stabbed Simcoe in the breast. Pope lived one hour by the wire's account, though the Harrison Times and a Missouri paper said he died almost at once. Simcoe was still alive the next morning with a wound described as fatal.

The dispatch closed by saying that "at last accounts" Lane was in the hands of a mob and was believed to have been lynched. A later news summary added that he "was seized by a mob, and it is supposed was taken away and lynched," without naming the place.

No report of Lane's death, an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage, and Simcoe's fate is not reported. The Harrison Times account, published more than two weeks later, made no mention of a mob. In Missouri, the Kahoka Herald reported that a Keokuk man identified Lane as "the detective of Clark county notoriety."

The story began as a special from Alma to the Little Rock Gazette and moved by wire, appearing on August 25 and 26 in papers from Pennsylvania and Illinois to Tennessee, California, Washington Territory and Wyoming. Headlines varied from "Fatal Fight Over a Game of Cards" in Lancaster to "Murder and Lynching" in Cheyenne and "Double Murder and Lynching" in Memphis, while the text kept the wire's hedge. Telegraph errors altered the names, giving the town as "Martinsburg" and the victims as "David Page," "Leonard Pope" and "Wm. Simcoe."

Weekly crime roundups compressed the report and dropped the qualification, one stating that "A mob lynched Lane last night" and another that the knifer "was taken in charge by a mob and hanged." Reprints ran as late as August 31 in Nebraska, and the Kahoka Herald remarked that Lane's "soul is probably now marching on." None of the coverage gave the race of anyone involved.

Whether Lane was killed is unsettled: the source dispatch only believed it, later roundups asserted it without new information, and the one Arkansas account found did not mention a mob at all. The Harrison Times also named the accused man Monroe Lane rather than Frank Lane.

bases: Every report of mob action describes a reported mob killing of an accused man (A1, A8, A18), though the wire said only that he was 'believed' lynched and the one Arkansas paper found mentions no mob (A25).

The card-game stabbing is reported independently by the Alma wire and the Harrison Times (A1, A25), but the mob seizure and reported lynching rest on the one Alma special to the Little Rock Gazette (A3), which every other report repeats or condenses (A8, A17, A18, A23).

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Alma wire verbatim under crime headlines such as 'A Deadly Affray' and 'Bloody Affair', keeping the 'believed' hedge on the lynching.
Weekly roundups dropped the hedge, stating 'A mob lynched Lane last night' or that he was 'taken in charge by a mob and hanged.'
The Kahoka Herald, reprinted in Missouri, treated the reported lynching lightly, saying Lane's 'soul is probably now marching on.'
